query: Starting from a W–Cu composite containing W particles or interconnected W ligaments within a Cu matrix, what single intervention could overcome phase separation and interfacial void formation, thereby improving thermal conductivity relative to the untreated composite under heat-transfer and irradiation conditions relevant to joints between W-based plasma-facing materials and Cu-based cooling components? Formulate one hypothesis that states the intervention, the proposed mechanism, the predicted comparative outcome, the applicable processing and service boundaries, supporting prior evidence, and a decisive falsification experiment.

generation.hypothesis: Depositing a uniform nanometer‐scale Ni coating on tungsten particles prior to composite fabrication will mitigate phase separation and prevent interfacial void formation in W–Cu composites, thereby enhancing their thermal conductivity under heat-transfer and irradiation conditions.
generation.material_initial_state: A W–Cu composite having tungsten particles (or interconnected tungsten ligaments) embedded in a copper matrix that, in the untreated state, suffers from phase separation and interfacial void formation.
generation.intervention: Apply a nanometer-scale Ni coating on the tungsten particles (or preform) using a technique such as physical vapor deposition or atomic layer deposition before combining with the Cu matrix and consolidating the composite.
generation.conditions: Processing via powder consolidation/sintering under conditions relevant to plasma-facing components and cooling joints, and service conditions including high heat flux and irradiation representative of fusion environments.
generation.structural_mediator: An interfacial Ni-rich layer that forms a solid solution or metallurgically bonded interface between the tungsten and Cu matrix.
generation.mechanism: The Ni coating reduces the interfacial energy mismatch between tungsten and copper, limits the tendency for phase separation by acting as a diffusion barrier and bonding promoter, and thereby minimizes void formation. This improved interfacial integrity promotes continuous heat transfer paths across the interface, even under irradiation and service thermal cycling.
generation.predicted_outcome: The Ni-coated composite will exhibit fewer interfacial voids and a more chemically and structurally stable interface, resulting in a measurable improvement in thermal conductivity (compared to the untreated composite) under relevant heat-transfer and irradiation conditions.
generation.baseline: The untreated W–Cu composite shows phase separation and interfacial void formation that inhibit effective thermal transport between tungsten and copper.
generation.boundary: This hypothesis applies to the processing and service regime of plasma-facing and cooling joint structures in nuclear fusion environments, where both high thermal gradients and irradiation effects are significant factors.
generation.uncertainty: The quantitative magnitude of the improvement in thermal conductivity and the precise diffusion dynamics at the Ni-mediated interface under prolonged irradiation remain uncertain and may depend on coating uniformity, thickness, and sintering conditions.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two groups of W–Cu composite samples: one group using tungsten particles with a deposited nanometer-scale Ni coating (via PVD/ALD) and a control group with untreated tungsten. Subject both groups to identical consolidation processes, followed by thermal cycling and irradiation protocols that mimic service conditions. Characterize the interfacial microstructure using SEM/TEM to quantify void formation and measure bulk thermal conductivity (e.g., by laser flash analysis) for both sets.
measurements: Interfacial microstructure and void density via electron microscopy
Thermal conductivity measurements under controlled thermal gradients
Diffusion profile analysis at the W–Cu interface using EDS or similar techniques
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the Ni-coated samples do not show a statistically significant reduction in interfacial void density or an improvement in thermal conductivity relative to the untreated control samples (within experimental uncertainty), then the hypothesis that the nanometer-scale Ni coating mitigates phase separation and improves thermal conduction is falsified.

cited_evidence.text: In this paper, a novel HEA/diamond composite was studied by magnetron sputtering Ti/Ni coating and the spark plasma sintering (SPS) method. A Ti/Ni coating (inner Ti and outer Ni) of diamond particles was realized by magnetron sputtering. An HEA/coated diamond interface was obtained, composed of the solid solution formed by diffusion between the HEA matrix and Ni element in the outer layer of diamond particles. The carbide formed by the reaction of Ti element with diamond particles. On the one hand, this interface can effectively reduce the interface energy between diamond and the HEA matrix and improve the bonding strength. On the other hand, the cracks and micro-holes on the interface after SPS can be filled by generated carbides to improve the density of the composites and improve the strength, toughness and other mechanical properties of the composites.

Diamond single crystal particles with Ti/Ni coatings were obtained by magnetron sputtering. The diamond gained more than 30% weight and the coating thickness was 10–20 μm. The interfacial diffusion and solid solution formation in coated diamond composites led to the increase of interfacial bonding strength. The interface bonding strength and mechanical properties of the composites without diamond coating decreased, due to the occurrence of graphitization at the interface and the formation of carbides. Compared with the composite with uncoated diamond, the density, hardness, transverse fracture strength and interfacial bonding properties of the composite with coated diamond were significantly improved. The wear resistance of the coated composites is obviously higher than that of the uncoated composites, because the coating on the diamond particles maintains a relatively complete crystal form in the SPS process and has a higher bonding strength with the HEA matrix. This improves the holding force of the matrix and gives full play to the excellent properties of the HEA.
